lead: Discourse is language beyond one sentence: a paragraph, a news report, a support chat. An utterance is one sentence used in context. A discourse is coherent when a reader can infer how its parts relate; it is cohesive when surface words and forms tie the parts together. Segmentation finds the units that carry those links. Summarisers, essay graders, chatbots and search engines use it to decide where one topic or move ends and the next begins.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for proposition meaning, Chapter 4.2 for sentence meaning, and Chapter 4.6 for predicate-argument links.

blocks.text: Cohesion is the visible glue between sentences. Halliday and Hasan list five types.

Reference points by a pronoun, demonstrative or article: 'Ravi missed the bus. He ran.' He refers back to Ravi. This is a cohesive device; finding Ravi as antecedent is coreference, covered in Chapter 4.8.
Substitution replaces one item with another: 'I wanted the window seat, but I got the aisle one.' One substitutes seat.
Ellipsis leaves a gap: 'Ravi ordered tea; Meera, coffee.' The second verb is omitted.
Conjunction links with a connector: 'It rained, so the match stopped.' So marks result.
Lexical cohesion uses word choice: repetition ('bus ... bus'), synonymy ('late ... delayed'), and collocation ('bus ... conductor').

Cohesion is not coherence. 'Ravi missed the bus. He was a mango.' has a pronoun but no sensible relation. Coherence is the inferred relation; cohesion is its surface marking. In 'Ravi missed the bus. He reached late.' the causal link is not marked by any conjunction; only the pronoun 'he' ties the two sentences, so cohesion is thin while the coherence is supplied by inference.
Writers use cohesion to guide the reader; readers use it to recover relations quickly. A machine can measure pronoun density, repeated words and connectors as features for coherence scoring.

A coherence relation names how two spans of text relate. Common names are Evidence, Result, Cause, Elaboration and Contrast. In Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST), most relations are asymmetric. The nucleus is the central span; the satellite supports it.

Take 'Ravi missed the bus. As a result, he reached the office late.' The first sentence gives the cause; the second gives the result. The relation is Result. The first sentence is the nucleus; the second is the satellite. The pronoun he is a cohesive link to Ravi, not the relation itself.

An RST tree groups spans. Leaves are elementary units, often sentences. Each internal node is a relation over a span. For this text the root is Result with two children. Spans are contiguous ranges of text: [1] and [2], then [1-2]. A larger report would nest more relations.

Names shift with the question. 'Ravi reached late because he missed the bus' can be labelled Cause; the facts are the same, but the nucleus is now the result. Evidence supports a claim: 'Ravi is late. He missed the bus.' Elaboration adds detail: 'Ravi missed the bus, the 7:10 to T. Nagar.' Contrast sets two spans against each other: 'Ravi missed the bus. Meera caught it.'

Contrast is one of the few multinuclear relations, so neither span is nucleus or satellite; both carry equal weight. Relations such as Evidence, Result, Cause and Elaboration are nucleus-satellite relations.

Cue phrases signal relations: because, so, however, for example, in fact, as a result. They help label relations and place boundaries. Ambiguity is common. 'Since' can mark time ('since Monday') or cause ('since he left early'). 'While' can mark time or contrast. 'And' can add or contrast. 'So what?' has so but no Result relation. A relation may also be implicit, with no cue at all. Discourse markers are cue phrases in talk, such as well, okay, you know; they manage turns and attention as well as relations.

Discourse segmentation cuts text into units that carry relations: sentences, clauses, paragraphs or topic blocks. Paragraph breaks help but are not always boundaries; a writer may break a paragraph in the middle of one argument. Cue-phrase segmentation starts a new unit at a strong cue such as 'However'. It is simple, but it misses implicit cues and can overfire inside quotations.

TextTiling uses lexical cohesion. Split the text into fixed-size token blocks. Score each pair of adjacent blocks by word overlap. A low score is a candidate boundary. TextTiling then computes a depth score at each gap from the drop in similarity against its neighbours and marks a boundary only where the depth score crosses a threshold. A standard score is cosine over word frequencies:
sim(b_i, b_j) = Σ_w tf(w, b_i) × tf(w, b_j) ÷ (√Σ_w tf(w, b_i)² × √Σ_w tf(w, b_j)²)
blocks.where: tf(w,b) is the count of word w in block b; the sums run over the vocabulary; sim is between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: Supervised segmentation treats each gap as a classification: features from words, cue phrases, punctuation and syntax predict boundary or not. Training needs labelled texts. Lexical chains track repeated related words across sentences; a chain break or a switch to a new chain can mark a new segment.

figure.caption: The tree shows the Result relation: missing the bus is the nucleus cause, reaching late is the satellite result, and the pronoun he points to Ravi.

spec.aria: An RST tree with root Result, nucleus Missed bus, and satellite Reached late.

examples.question: Segment this text into two units and draw an RST tree: 'Ravi missed the bus. As a result, he reached the office late.' Name the coherence relation and list two cohesive devices. Say whether removing 'As a result' changes the relation.
steps: Sentence boundaries give two units: U1 = 'Ravi missed the bus.' and U2 = 'As a result, he reached the office late.'
The cue phrase 'As a result' marks a result; the relation is Result.
RST tree: root Result, left child U1 with edge nucleus, right child U2 with edge satellite. The span of the root is U1-U2.
Cohesive devices: (a) reference: he refers to Ravi; (b) conjunction: As a result links the sentences. Lexical repetition is absent.

Remove 'As a result': the two sentences remain coherent for most readers, because missing a bus and arriving late invite a causal inference. The relation is still Result, but now it is implicit, not cued. A strict system may label it Unknown without the cue.
examples.answer: Two units U1 and U2; root Result with nucleus U1 and satellite U2; devices are reference (he → Ravi) and conjunction (As a result); removing the cue keeps the inferred Result relation but removes the explicit cue.

traps: Cohesion is not coherence: pronouns can appear in nonsense.
RST relations are not sentence-level grammar relations; a causal clause can be inside one sentence or across two.
Cue phrases are ambiguous: 'since' can mark time or cause.
A paragraph break can be stylistic, not a discourse boundary.
A relation label depends on the writer's intended span, not only on word order.

quiz.q: Name the five cohesion types of Halliday and Hasan.
quiz.a: Reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, lexical cohesion.

quiz.q: Why can a text be cohesive but not coherent? Give one example.
quiz.a: Cohesive links can be present without a sensible relation. 'Ravi missed the bus. He was a mango.' has a pronoun but no coherent meaning.

quiz.q: For 'Meera ordered tea. Ravi, coffee.' identify the cohesive device and the words left out.
quiz.a: Ellipsis; the second clause omits 'ordered' before coffee.

quiz.q: In 'Ravi missed the bus. However, he reached late.' what relation does 'However' signal? Is the text coherent? Explain.
quiz.a: 'However' signals Contrast. But the second sentence is not contrary to the first: missing the bus explains why he was late, so the contrast cue misfires and the text reads oddly. It becomes properly coherent only if the second span is genuinely unexpected, e.g. 'Ravi missed the bus. However, he reached the office on time.' The passage is understandable as cause-result, but that relation is not what 'However' marks.

quiz.q: Define nucleus and satellite in RST.
quiz.a: The nucleus is the central span; the satellite supports it in an asymmetric relation.

quiz.q: Give one reason a paragraph break may not be a discourse boundary.
quiz.a: A writer may break a paragraph for style in the middle of one argument; the relation continues across the break.

quiz.q: A text repeats many words and pronouns but each sentence contradicts the last. Is it cohesive or coherent? Explain.
quiz.a: It is cohesive, because surface links are present. It is not coherent, because the reader cannot build consistent relations between the propositions.

beyond: Not for the exam. Discourse parsing builds full RST trees with neural models and is used in summarisation and essay scoring. Search 'discourse coherence modelling', 'RST Discourse Treebank', and 'TextTiling' for entry points. Recent work links discourse structure to long-document question answering.
